title: Shakuntala at court
hook: Shakuntala walks into the king's hall with his son, he says he's never seen her, and she answers with an old verse
carry: a child is your own self, born again

segments.voice: Yesterday, marriage by your own choice has a place in dharma: Shakuntala's gandharva marriage, a yes of her own choosing, on a promise spoken aloud.
screen: `MARRIAGE BY YOUR OWN CHOICE HAS A PLACE IN DHARMA.`

segments.voice: A crowded royal hall, and a woman holding a boy by the hand. No one ever came from the city, so Kanva has sent Shakuntala and her son to the king. She bows and says it plainly: this is your son. Make him your heir, as you promised me at the hermitage. King Dushyanta looks at her and says he doesn't know her, never married her, has no idea who she is. Everyone is watching. What does she do now?
screen: `I DON'T REMEMBER YOU.` → `THIS IS YOUR SON.` → `EVERYONE IS WATCHING.`

segments.voice: For a moment, the epic says, she can't move. She stands there stunned, ashamed and furious at once. Then she speaks, for a long time. Here is some of it, in paraphrase. First, witnesses. You think you're alone with what you did, she tells him, but the sun and the moon, the wind and fire, the earth and the sky, your own heart, all of them saw. Then the boy. She reminds the king of an old Vedic verse: from my limbs you are born, from my heart you arise; you are my own self, called son. When the king answers with insults about her mother and her birth in the forest, she turns his words around: you see others' faults as small as a mustard seed, and miss your own, as big as a bilva fruit. She never begs. Then a voice from the sky tells the king she speaks the truth, and the boy is his. Only then does Dushyanta take them in. Here's the teaching. That verse is older than the story. In the Vedic household rites, a father says it over his newborn, and again when he comes home from a journey and breathes in the scent of his child's head. In Hindu thought, a child isn't a possession or a stranger. A child is your own self, born again, and no father can say he doesn't know his own self. Plenty of Hindu parents and grandparents still greet a child by breathing in the top of their head, whether or not they know the verse. The old rite ends with a blessing: live a hundred autumns.
screen: `STUNNED, THEN SHE SPEAKS` · `THE SUN AND MOON WERE WITNESSES` · `YOU ARE MY OWN SELF, CALLED SON` · `A VOICE FROM THE SKY AGREES` · then, large: `A CHILD IS YOUR OWN SELF, BORN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who is part of you: a child, a niece or nephew, a younger cousin, or the person who first held you that way. Picture the old greeting, breathing in the top of their head, and on each out-breath say inwardly: you are part of me. If you pray, you can bless them the way the rite does: live a hundred autumns.
Shakuntala. The woman who stood in a king's hall and reminded him that his son was his own self, until the sky itself agreed.
Your line: a child is your own self, born again. Shakuntala made a king remember it. Back tomorrow, same hill.

screen: `DAY 1351 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE GUEST AT THE HERMITAGE.`

howItsDone: Hindus know Shakuntala's speech at court from the Mahabharata's first book, the Adi Parva; the same story is retold in the poet Kalidasa's later play, which changes how the king comes to forget her.

original.note: Sanskrit: the epic explains her name from shakunta, bird, for the birds that guarded her as a baby.

chat.meaning: Shakuntala reminds the king of the Vedic verse: from my limbs you are born, from my heart; you are my own self, called son. The old household rites have a father say it over his child and breathe in the child's head on coming home.

tie.story: When King Dushyanta denied his son, Shakuntala reminded him of the old verse: a child is the father's own self, born again.
tie.friend: Priya can tell Sam it's a blessing, not a weird habit: when Dad breathes in her head, he's greeting his own self in her.
tie.you: who greets you like you're part of them?

Dushyanta.meaning: the king who says he doesn't know her

bilva.meaning: a large fruit, set here against a tiny mustard seed

Kanva.meaning: the sage who raised her and sent her to court

atman.meaning: the self; the verse calls a child the parent's own self

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Shakuntala at Dushyanta's court; his denial; her speech: the witnesses, the verse 'from my limbs you are born… you are my own self, called son', the son as a mirror, the mustard seed and the bilva fruit; the king's insults; the voice from the sky)
Kaushitaki Upanishad, ch. 2 (the father, back from a journey, smells his son's head and says 'from my limbs you are born…'; section numbering varies); Grihya Sutras (the birth rite)
